leading_positions.synthesis: Five of eight members state the optical lattice clock (Katori and Ye) as their sole preferred prize part in round 1. They share the same two names, the argument that the magic-wavelength idea plus Ye's performance frontier gives independent reproduction at several laboratories, and the view that the work yields physics (redshift, constants, dark-matter couplings) and not only a better clock. They differ on how much weight to give overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, on how far parallel strontium-clock groups (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) are a problem for a two-name credit, and on whether to wait for the redefinition of the second. Danielsson and Johansson say they opened with other candidates (EHT and circuit QED) and moved to B056 after reading the openings; Pearce moved it from fifth to first.

Two members prefer topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as the sole prize part. Both stress a clean Z2 mechanism confirmed independently over about fifteen years, and both name the same attribution weakness: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (and the 3D and ARPES contributions) lie outside the trio. They differ on emphasis: Eriksson stresses a new class of quantum matter and calls recognition arguably overdue, while Mehlig calls it a distinct, experimentally anchored achievement relative to the 2016 prize but says he would not oppose a later year and warns of his own theory bias. Both list B056 as an alternative.

One member prefers spherical-aberration correction in transmission electron microscopy (Rose, Urban, Haider) as the sole prize part, on the grounds of a verified instrument invention that broke the Scherzer limit and a documented credit chain. She herself names the main weaknesses: it is an instrument prize, only three members ranked it in the opening, the Nion STEM corrector (Batson, Dellby, Krivanek) is a parallel line outside the credited names, and she flags her own field closeness and possible recusal. She lists B056 and B003 as alternatives and asks whether B056 is stronger than she allowed.

areas_of_agreement: All eight members state a single-part prize configuration; no member proposes a shared prize split across two ballot IDs.
Every member ranked B056 in the opening, and all five of its supporters name the same two laureates; Eriksson, Mehlig and Olsson list it as an alternative to their own first choice.
Independent reproduction is treated as decisive wherever it exists: members who support B056 or B007 cite confirmation by several independent groups over many years as the reason the claim is mature.
Members across fields name the same gap for each leading candidate: parallel clock groups for B056, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang for B007, and the Nion corrector for B032.

Members who support B056 or B007 each state their own candidate's main weakness unprompted, and Danielsson and Kroll say the case for the clock should rest on the physics it opens (redshift, constants, dark matter) and not on engineering alone.
scientific_disputes: Whether the optical lattice clock is a discovery about nature or an excellent invention and measurement capability; all five supporters raise this, and Eriksson explicitly defers to the atomic physicists.

Whether the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize leave the lattice clock enough distinct standing, versus reading it as a refinement of recognised precision spectroscopy (raised by Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Pearce).
Whether the 2016 topology prize makes time-reversal-invariant topological insulators a distinct discovery (Mehlig says yes; Eriksson and Danielsson want the committee to be sure).
Whether an instrument and method prize such as B032 ranks as fundamental physics against candidates that test fundamental physics directly (raised by Olsson against her own preference).

Whether IceCube (B003) is a discovery or still at evidence level for source identification (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, Galactic plane); it appears as an alternative for Danielsson, Olsson and Pearce but is no member's first choice.
attribution_disputes: B056: Katori and Ye are the only names proposed, but Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE teams are cited by several members as decisive contributors who cannot fit in a two-name credit.

B007: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe quantum-well prediction that guided Molenkamp's experiment; Eriksson also asks whether Mele or another person is the right third name, and the 3D topological insulator and ARPES work (Fu, Moore, Balents, Roy, Hasan) is only partly covered.

B032: Krivanek and the Nion STEM corrector (Batson, Dellby, Krivanek, 2002) and Zach's early SEM corrector work sit outside Rose, Urban and Haider; Olsson also asks whether the Wolf Prize record counts as evidence.
B003: Danielsson, in responding to Pearce, raises the AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal lineage and the scale of the IceCube collaboration as making a two-name credit (Halzen, Karle) contestable.
B034 (alternative for Kroll and Lindroth): overlapping credit among Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich, with Chu already honoured in 1997, is described as harder to defend than the clock credit.
maturity_disputes: Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the SI second before recognising B056: Kroll judges waiting unnecessary, Danielsson sees no need to wait, Johansson and Lindroth list it as an open question, and Pearce notes it could be argued.
B007 is described as mature and arguably overdue by Eriksson and timely by Mehlig, but both note a possible interaction with the 2016 prize and, for Mehlig, with the 2025 circuits prize.

B058 (circuit QED) is not preferred by any member in round 1; Johansson, who opened with it first, now judges the clock the stronger choice and says the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize is close in subject.
B003: whether IceCube source-identification results will mature within a few years, as Pearce asks.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Johansson directs the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and works in the field of B058 (circuit QED); he flags possible recusal or extra caution on B058 and says he did not rely on it in his configuration.
Olsson works in transmission electron microscopy and was IFSM President; she asks the committee to consider whether she should recuse herself on B032, her preferred ballot.
Lindroth flags field closeness to B034 (atom interferometry) and B019 (squeezed light), and long collaboration with Anne L'Huillier, none of which concerns B056.

Kroll notes membership of the same broad AMO community as B056 without a link to Katori or Ye, close knowledge of the quantum-memory field (B023, not shortlisted), and institutional overlap of WACQT leadership with Johansson's Chalmers, which bears on B058.
Mehlig notes a shared Gothenburg physics environment with Johansson and Olsson (Chalmers) and a possible theory-side bias toward B007.

Pearce (chair) notes that IceCube lies in his own field of astroparticle physics, though he is not an IceCube member, and that he is not an atomic physicist and relies on Lindroth and Kroll for B056 detail.
No member discloses a specific personal or institutional link to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp.
questions_for_round2: B056: Do the atomic physicists (Lindroth, Kroll) judge the lattice clock distinct enough from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize to stand as a discovery-level achievement, and what specific physical results beyond better accuracy would they cite?

B056: Is Katori and Ye the fairest two-name credit given Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, and can a citation wording honour the lattice clock invention without implying that others did not contribute?
B056: Does the committee wait for the redefinition of the SI second, or is the performance already confirmed well enough that timing is not a reason to delay?
B007: Can a citation be worded for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp that does not implicitly exclude Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and what is the status of the 3D and ARPES contributions in the credited trio?
B007: How much weight does the 2016 topology prize carry against a second topology-related award, and does the 2025 circuits prize alter timing?

B032: Does the primary record on priority between the Rose, Haider and Urban correctors and the Nion STEM corrector support a three-name credit, and should Olsson participate in that question given her flag?
B003: What would settle the IceCube attribution question (AMANDA and earlier lineage versus Halzen and Karle), and is source identification mature enough for this year?
If B056 and B007 are both judged sound on merit and attribution, what criterion should decide between them: breadth of support, credit clarity, or timing?
summary.chair_observation: Round 1 shows five members for B056, two for B007 and one for B032, each as a single prize part, and all supporters of the leading candidates volunteer the same attribution weakness in their own files. Several members changed position after reading the openings, so the count should be tested in round 2 and not taken as settled. The open items are the discovery-versus-capability question for B056, the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap for B007, and the recusal questions flagged by Olsson and Johansson. These are recorded here without a ruling.
